newsitem.title: USA: Nintendo offers Nintendo 64 in U.S. market.
newsitem.headline: Nintendo offers Nintendo 64 in U.S. market.

text.p: Nintendo of America Inc., firing the latest shot in the video games arms race, said Monday it was introducing its newest player, the Nintendo 64, to the U.S. market for $199.95.

The subsidiary of Japan's Nintendo Co. Ltd. said it believed it will sell its entire supply, more than 1 million units, and will push to sell 3 million games in North America over the final six months of its fiscal year ending March 1997.
Even before the official launch, Nintendo executives began trumpeting strong consumer demand that had stores selling the player Friday to satisfy pent-up demand.

"We shipped about 350,000 units initially, and 50 percent of that was pre-sold," Perrin Kaplan, director of corporate affairs, said in a recent interview. "We're very sure the supply is not going to meet demand." Targets call for 600,000 to players to be sold by Christmas.
Nintendo 64, or N64, is the company's newest weapon in the war for market share in the $4 billion market for video game hardware and software.
Questions remaining include how interested game developers will be in creating the relatively more expensive cartridges for the player and what games will be hits.
Nintendo 64, a 64-bit system, is Nintendo's answer to Sony Corp.'s Playstaton and Sega Enterprises Ltd.'s Saturn, less powerful 32-bit game systems that were successfully launched last fall.
Nintendo had intended to have Nintendo 64 ready for consumers in 1995 but delayed the launch to perfect its player and its lead game, Super Mario 64.

The Super Mario game, in which the popular plumber flies, is the key to Nintendo's $54 million promotional game plan for Nintendo 64. Games based on the little plumber have sold millions of copies on various other Nintendo game platforms.

Nintendo 64 was developed and licensed jointly with computer maker Silicon Graphics Inc. In addition to Super Mario 64, games include PilotWings 64, a 3-D flight simulation, Nintendo said. Each sells for $69.95.

While Saturn and Playstation are based on compact disc technology for storage, Nintendo 64 uses cartridges, which are faster to play but more expensive to produce and riskier to keep in inventory. Developers have been reluctant to adopt the 64-bit technology.
